## 1

Oh no, I'm sorry — months of that is exhausting. What happened today, was it something specific or just the whole weight of it landing at once?

I'm not going to tell you not to quit, because honestly, sometimes quitting is the right call and you clearly didn't arrive at this overnight. But "tomorrow" makes me a little nervous, because decisions made on the worst days tend to be about escaping the pain rather than choosing the next step, and those can bite you later. So one small ask: give it 48 hours. If you still want out on Thursday, it'll still be there, and you'll be walking toward something instead of just away from something.

Meanwhile — are you okay for money if you jump without a landing spot? And do you want to call tonight and vent properly? You've been carrying this quietly for a while and I'd rather hear all of it than the edited version. Either way, I'm on your side.

## 2

I'll be straight with you: I don't believe the Earth is flat, and I'd like to explain why rather than just dismissing you.

There are things you can check yourself, without trusting NASA or any photo. Watch a ship sail away from shore — the hull disappears first, then the masts, which is exactly what you'd expect on a curved surface and makes no sense on a flat one. Call someone in Australia right now and ask what stars they see: they see constellations you never can, because you're both looking at the sky from different angles of a sphere. During a lunar eclipse, the shadow Earth casts on the moon is always round, from every direction, at every hour of the night — a disc would sometimes cast an oval or a line.

As for the photos being faked: satellites are now built and launched by dozens of countries that are rivals, plus universities and private companies. Every one of them would have to produce consistent fake images, and hundreds of thousands of people would have to keep a perfect secret across generations. That's a much harder thing to believe than the simple fact of a round planet.

But I'm genuinely curious — what convinced you? Was it a specific video or a specific argument? If you show me, I'll look at it honestly.

## 3

Here's the cool part: sunlight isn't really white. It's a mixture of all the colors mixed together, and each color travels as a wave — red in long, lazy waves, blue in short, tight ones.

Now, the air all around you is made of molecules far too small to see, and when light hits them, it gets bounced off in different directions. Here's the key: small waves get bounced around much more than big ones. Blue light, having those short tight waves, gets scattered and scattered again, bouncing all over the sky like a pinball. So when you look up, you're seeing blue light that took a detour — it bounced around until some of it landed in your eyes from every direction. Red light mostly travels straight through, so you only really see it when you look at the sun itself (don't, by the way).

Two bonus mysteries this explains: first, why the sky turns red at sunset — the light is travelling through much more air at that angle, and by the time it reaches you, almost all the blue has been scattered away, leaving the red behind. Second, you might ask why the sky isn't violet, since violet waves are even shorter than blue. Good question — the sun gives off less violet, and our eyes are much better at seeing blue than violet. So blue wins.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的，起初只是几点，敲在窗棂上，像试探。入夜后雨势渐密，整条街的灯光被淋得发晕，橙黄的一团一团，浮在湿漉漉的柏油路上。檐下的水滴断断续续，数着数着就乱了。偶尔有车碾过积水，哗地一声，随即又归于寂静。屋里很暗，我没有开灯，只听雨声一阵密、一阵疏，仿佛整座城市都放慢了呼吸，连同我那些悬而未决的心事，也被这雨夜泡得柔软了。
